title: Gold Price Forecasting
bullets: Applied Time Series Analysis | B.Tech AI Semester VII | 2026-27
ARIMA / SARIMA analysis with an INR-per-gram application
18K, 20K, 22K and 24K fine-gold estimates
Priyanshu Modak (I080) | Vishesh Dokania (I019) | Parth Zanwar (I074)
notes: Good morning, Professor. Our project studies daily gold futures with the complete ATSA workflow. We first build and evaluate the model in USD per troy ounce, then convert forecasts into rupees per gram for four purities. We will show measured results and limitations. The analysis snapshot ends October 26, 2026.

title: The questions we investigated
bullets: Can past prices support useful daily forecasts?
Does ARIMA or weekly SARIMA improve on tomorrow = today?
How does uncertainty change with the forecast horizon?
How can forecasts be displayed for Indian users?
notes: This is a univariate time-series study with a demonstrable application. Success means correct preprocessing, a defensible evaluation and clear uncertainty. It does not require the most complex model to win. The Indian-price output estimates metal value, not a city-specific retail quote.

Artifacts: charts, CSVs, fitted model and metadata

title: Cleaning and chronological split
bullets: Sort/deduplicate; require positive numeric closes
Forward-fill 111 missing weekdays: 3.60%
Regular series: 3,082 business weekdays
Train 2,982 through 08 Jun | Test 100 from 09 Jun 2026
notes: Forward fill carries the last known price; no future price is used. Generic Monday-Friday indexing includes exchange holidays and introduces some zero returns. The hold-out consists of regularised weekdays, not strictly 100 observed trading sessions. Random splitting would mix past and future. The grid is fitted on training only.

title: EDA: price levels and dependence
bullets: Source mean: USD 1,966.46 per troy ounce
Source-price standard deviation: USD 956.73
Lagged prices move together; returns need separate study
A rising price level alone does not establish predictability
notes: Explain the level and rolling mean from the saved chart. These descriptive statistics use the 2,971 source observations before weekday filling. Consecutive price levels can be highly correlated simply because both share a stochastic trend. That is not proof of an exploitable forecasting signal. Lag scatter plots are saved separately.

title: EDA: distribution and heavy tails
bullets: Source-return excess kurtosis: 7.7843
Jarque-Bera rejects normality; QQ tails depart
Source-return annualised volatility: about 16.8%
Heavy tails limit unqualified Gaussian interval claims
notes: The QQ plot compares empirical return quantiles to normal quantiles. Tail departures suggest more extreme moves than the normal reference. Volatility is descriptive historical information, not a guaranteed future estimate. Normality failure matters especially for uncertainty assumptions; it does not automatically invalidate every point forecast.

title: Stationarity: opposite null hypotheses
bullets: Price: ADF p=.9755; KPSS lower reported bound .01
Log price: ADF p=.9897; KPSS lower bound .01
Log return: ADF p about 6.83e-27; KPSS upper bound .10
The sample supports first-differenced logs: d=1
notes: ADF has a unit-root null; KPSS has a stationarity null. Small ADF and non-small KPSS support stationarity in this sample. ADF non-rejection does not prove a unit root. A printed zero is rounded, not a literally zero probability. KPSS reports tabulated bounds. Mean-process stationarity can coexist with changing conditional variance.

title: Transformation and selected equation
bullets: z(t) = log(P(t)); r(t) = z(t) - z(t-1)
ARIMA(p,1,q) models short-memory dynamics in r(t)
Selected: z(t) = z(t-1) + drift + innovation
exp(log forecast) is a conditional median
notes: Logs express proportional changes and keep inverse forecasts positive. First differences remove the integrated level. With p=q=0 this is a log random walk with drift. A mean on the price scale would require a distribution-appropriate bias correction, such as exp(mu+v/2) for Gaussian log uncertainty. The app reports the exponentiated location without that correction.

title: Seasonality: examine rather than assume
bullets: Strength: 5 days .0002 | 21 days .0084
252-business-day strength: .1747
Annual decomposition is descriptive evidence only
A weekly SARIMA competitor is evaluated
notes: A 252-day period approximates an annual business-day cycle rather than an exact calendar year. Classical decomposition imposes a periodic structure and uses centred calculations, so it is exploratory here. We did not evaluate every seasonal order or annual SARIMA. The actual forecasting competitor uses seasonal order (1,0,1,5).

title: ACF/PACF and model identification
bullets: AR: PACF cutoff; ACF usually decays
MA: ACF cutoff; PACF usually decays
ARMA: both decay; seasonal spikes motivate SARIMA
Squared-return dependence motivates variance analysis
notes: These are finite-sample heuristics, not automatic proofs. Some spikes occur by chance across many inspected lags. AR and MA terms act on the differenced log process inside ARIMA. Moving-average innovation terms are not the same as a rolling mean. The squared-return plot concerns volatility rather than just mean predictability.

title: The recorded 25-model search
bullets: p=0..4; d=1; q=0..4 -> 25 candidate orders
Same training log-price series; drift in every candidate
AIC selects (1,1,4); BIC selects (0,1,0)
Convergence warnings occurred: rankings need a caveat
notes: AIC is 2k minus twice log likelihood; BIC is k log n minus twice log likelihood. BIC penalises complexity more at this sample size. Negative scores are valid. The notebook keeps finite scores and does not persist a convergence flag for every candidate. Therefore do not claim 25 certified converged fits or an optimum over all possible ARIMA models.

title: Two evaluation designs
bullets: One-step: forecast, then observe for later predictions
Model parameters stay fixed during hold-out updates
Fixed-origin: forecast 100 dates with no test updates
The app refits available history and forecasts 5..60 weekdays
notes: Appending test observations with refit=False and obtaining one-step predictions updates model states with past observations while retaining training parameters. This differs from forecasting the whole test path at once. The reported RMSE comparison is one-step; do not call it 30-day-ahead RMSE. The separate fixed-origin chart addresses the harder multi-step problem.

title: Measured performance: naive wins RMSE
bullets: Naive 60.5337 | BIC ARIMA 60.6723 USD/oz
AIC ARIMA 60.6684 | SARIMA 60.6085 USD/oz
BIC MAPE 1.0778%; directional agreement 49%
HAC loss-difference p=.4639: BIC ARIMA vs naive
notes: State the result directly. Naive has the lowest RMSE, while AIC ARIMA has slightly lower MAE/MAPE. Different metrics can rank models differently. BIC is a prespecified simple-model choice, not the hold-out RMSE winner. A non-small p-value fails to detect a loss difference; it does not prove equality or market efficiency. MAPE is not classification accuracy.

title: Intervals and residual diagnostics
bullets: Fixed-origin 100-day interval coverage: 94/100
Residual Ljung-Box p=.08397 at lag 10; .000589 at lag 20
ARCH-LM p about 6.28e-45; normality rejected
Longer-lag dependence and changing variance remain
notes: This is a single correlated path, not independent proof of interval calibration. Residual diagnostics use the training fit with the first initialisation residual removed. It would be false to say all assumptions passed. Longer-lag correlation, squared-residual dependence and non-normality limit strong adequacy claims. The nominal 95% bands depend on model assumptions.

title: Optional GARCH volatility extension
bullets: Variance = omega + alpha*past shock^2 + beta*past variance
Training alpha=.0359; beta=.9583; sum=.9942
Student-t innovations fitted to percentage log returns
Final normal-quantile bands remain approximate
notes: ARIMA models conditional mean; GARCH models changing conditional variance. Persistence near one indicates slow decay in the fitted variance process. The final band sums predicted daily variances and uses 1.96 around the ARIMA log forecast. It is not an exact Student-t interval or a jointly simulated ARIMA-GARCH system. The interactive app does not offer a GARCH engine.

title: Final saved forecast
bullets: Selected ARIMA refitted on all 3,082 observations
30-business-day snapshot saved as a forecast CSV
27 Oct 2026 median: USD 4,039.29 per troy ounce
ARIMA interval: USD 3,957.84 to 4,122.41
notes: This is the saved October 26 analysis snapshot. A later live app can differ because of new data or the default ten-year app history versus the notebook start in 2015. It is not a contradiction. Demonstrate outputs/forecast_next_30_days.csv and explain the difference between a point median and an uncertainty interval.

title: INR per gram and all four karats
bullets: INR/g = USD/oz x INR/USD / 31.1034768 x fineness
Dated automatic FX or a positive manual override
Same factor scales history, median and both bounds
notes: Precious metals use a troy ounce, not the ordinary ounce. We use linked BIS fineness values: 22K=.916 rather than exactly 22/24 and 24K fine gold=.999 rather than exactly one. These are four purity scalings of one underlying forecast, not four independently trained models. Units and conversion assumptions are visible in the app.

title: What the Indian-price display means
bullets: Selected FX is held fixed for all future dates
History is revalued at that same selected rate
Future FX risk, GST, duties and making charges excluded
Metal-value estimates are not jewellery-shop quotations
notes: The displayed history is not an observed historical INR series. We would need date-aligned historical FX and future FX modelling to build that. At fixed USD gold prices a 10% rise in INR per USD scales every INR value by 10%, without changing native-model AIC/BIC. Location, premiums, taxes and making charges explain differences from a retail quote.

title: Professor demo: deliberate actions
bullets: Start 24K, 30 weekdays, ARIMA(0,1,0)
Switch 22K -> 20K -> 18K; inspect comparison table
Compare horizons 5 and 60; change FX and order
Export CSVs; explain valid upload and real-data fallback
notes: Predict each effect before clicking. Purity scales the output but does not invent a new price pattern. Longer horizons create additional rows and generally broader uncertainty for the selected random walk. Changing history or order triggers a model change and can be slow. Show saved results at the end, including the naive baseline and failed diagnostic tests. Do not delete data to stage an outage.

title: All finite setting combinations
bullets: 4 karats x 13 history values x 56 horizons x 72 orders
72 orders = 6 p choices x 2 d choices x 6 q choices
209,664 discrete tuples are fully enumerated
Enumeration is not 209,664 executed model fits
notes: History ranges 3..15, horizon 5..60, p/q 0..5 and d 1 or 2. The compressed CSV lists all finite setting tuples. title: Decision combinations and evidence
bullets: ADF rejects + KPSS does not: stationarity supported
ADF does not reject + KPSS rejects: investigate differencing
Both reject or neither rejects: evidence is inconclusive
ARCH rejection: inspect variance, not just mean dynamics
notes: Avoid automatic test-based buttons. Examine trend specification, sample size, structural breaks and diagnostics. If AIC improves but hold-out RMSE worsens, complexity may not generalise. Repeatedly tuning to the same hold-out biases conclusions. The walkthrough includes decision tables, the complete order catalogue and professor Q&A.

title: Limitations and next steps
bullets: No demonstrated RMSE advantage over naive
Convergence flags and rolling-origin checks need improvement
No forecast of FX, interest rates, inflation or news
Next: aligned INR target, trading calendar, calibrated intervals
notes: Separate completed work from future work. Proposed improvements include storing and filtering convergence outcomes, multiple rolling origins, horizon-specific accuracy, aligned FX and an exchange-aware calendar. Prophet, LSTM, annual SARIMA and exogenous regressors are not implemented and have no results in this project.

title: Backup: order families and trend rules
bullets: (0,1,0): random walk with log drift
(p,1,0): AR in differences | (0,1,q): MA in differences
(p,1,q): ARMA in first-differenced log prices
App d=2 is available; its deterministic trend is n
notes: For d=1 the app uses trend t, giving drift in first differences. For d=2 it uses no deterministic trend. So d comparisons change both differencing and trend assumptions. d=0, seasonal order controls and GARCH selection are not offered in the app. The 72-order table records these rules.

title: Backup: failure and fallback combinations
bullets: Gold live fails + real cache: labelled cached prices
FX live fails + snapshot: dated saved exchange rate
No FX source: require a positive manual rate
Bad CSV / insufficient data: stop rather than fabricate
notes: Evidence labels distinguish verified UI checks from code-reviewed or planned scenarios. Required CSV columns are Date and Close; units must be USD per troy ounce. Invalid numeric and nonpositive prices are filtered; at least 100 valid observations are needed. Dates are sorted and duplicates keep the last. Fit warnings are not always hard failures.

title: Backup: four questions to answer precisely
bullets: Does 1.1% MAPE mean 98.9% accuracy?
Why can naive outperform fitted ARIMA?
Why does the app differ from the notebook?
Why is a 24K result different from a jeweller quote?
notes: Answers: MAPE is average relative error, not classification accuracy. Weak predictable structure and estimation error can make naive competitive. A new window, order, data date or FX setting changes the app output. Jewellery quotes include local/tax/product effects absent from a futures-derived metal estimate. Never turn these results into unsupported trading claims.
